title: Jeannie's Visit

jokes.text: Larry apologizes for pulling away from the double-cheek kiss, explaining he's American and 'always just happy with one kiss' and 'I figure the second one's... I'm gonna somehow get hurt.'
jokes.setup: Larry awkwardly explains why he recoiled from Tatjana's European double-cheek greeting kiss
jokes.punchline: He's so conditioned to receiving emotional injury that even a second kiss feels like an incoming blow
jokes.explanation: Classic Larry Sanders self-revealing neurosis delivered under the guise of a polite social explanation. The joke works because it's specific to Larry's damaged psyche — he's so emotionally beaten down that physical affection reads as a threat. Strong character integration.

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: My next guest, I'm sure you'll recognize. She is an inter... I can't even say this... she's an internationally known model and actress.

jokes.text: Larry: 'Usually a kiss on one side and a hit on the other.' Then pivots: 'But that's a very european thing, isn't it?'
jokes.setup: Larry has just confessed he panicked at the double-kiss because he expected to get hit
jokes.punchline: He treats his traumatized relationship history as a casual social observation, then immediately redirects to Tatjana's Europeanness to escape the vulnerability
jokes.explanation: The pivot is perfectly Larry — he confesses something genuinely dark about himself and then immediately course-corrects into a talk-show host platitude. The structural beat of 'confess → deflect' is the engine of a lot of Larry comedy.

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: I'm American, and I'm used to only kissing on one cheek. That's OK. Second of all, just being who I am, I'm always just happy with one kiss

jokes.text: Larry, trying to recover from not knowing Malmö, says 'I love Oslo' — which is in Norway.
jokes.setup: Tatjana tells Larry she's from Malmö, Sweden; Larry has clearly never heard of it and fumbles
jokes.punchline: He confidently name-drops Oslo — wrong country — revealing he's bluffing his cosmopolitan talk-show host persona entirely
jokes.explanation: Perfect encapsulation of Larry's insecurity masked by false confidence. The joke is economical and specific — he doesn't just say 'I don't know Sweden,' he overcompensates with a wrong-country capital. Tatjana's correction 'Yes, it's Norway' lands the kicker cleanly.

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: I figure the second one's... I'm gonna somehow get hurt. Usually a kiss on one side and a hit on the other.

jokes.text: Beverly panics that Jeannie Sanders is coming up in the elevator. Paula asks 'Jeannie who?' Beverly: 'Jeannie Sanders, Larry's ex-wife.'
jokes.setup: Beverly bursts in with urgent news about someone named Jeannie
jokes.punchline: Paula's blank 'Jeannie who?' — she either doesn't know or is deliberately obtuse — and Beverly's exasperated clarification signals the audience that this arrival is a crisis
jokes.explanation: Functional exposition joke that also establishes the comedy of Beverly's alarm. The 'Jeannie who?' beat is mildly amusing but not especially crafted — it's a standard sitcom clarification gag.

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: If you were asian, we would have bowed.

jokes.text: Larry to Tatjana: 'Wow, that is so rare to find someone else who likes Italian food.'
jokes.setup: Tatjana says she likes cooking Italian food
jokes.punchline: Larry's faux-astonished response treats one of the world's most popular cuisines as an exotic discovery — pure empty talk-show enthusiasm
jokes.explanation: Sharp satirical jab at the vacuous enthusiasm of talk-show host performance. Larry's line is so perfectly hollow it could be a textbook example of manufactured celebrity intimacy. Economy is excellent — the joke does its work in one sentence.

dialogue.line: I love oslo.
That's in norway.
Yes, it's norway.

jokes.text: Artie, informed that Jeannie Sanders has arrived, says: 'No, I'm asking the guy with one eye in row 6. I don't think he knows either.'
jokes.setup: Beverly tells Artie that Jeannie Sanders is here; he rhetorically asks what she's doing there
jokes.punchline: Artie's sardonic answer to his own rhetorical question by invoking a one-eyed audience member as his hypothetical informant
jokes.explanation: Classic Artie Rip Torn delivery — the specificity of 'the guy with one eye in row 6' is what elevates this from a generic brush-off to a genuine character moment. Only Artie would construct that particular sardonic edifice. Strong originality and character integration.

dialogue.line: Paula! Paula, you gotta help me. Jeannie's coming up in the elevator.

jokes.text: Artie, on learning Jeannie is here AND there's a juggler who hit himself with a bowling ball: 'First we have the damn juggler who bangs his head with a bowling ball, and now this.'
jokes.setup: Artie is being hit with two crises simultaneously — a bloody on-stage accident and the ex-wife showing up
jokes.punchline: He lists them as equivalent logistical problems, with the arrival of the ex-wife implied to be equally or more disastrous than a juggler bleeding on stage
jokes.explanation: The comedy is in Artie treating an ex-wife visit as equivalent to a bloody stage accident. It's also a great worldbuilding moment — the juggler with the bowling ball is briefly glimpsed as a chaotic real-world intrusion that Artie absorbs with weary professionalism.

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: Wow, that is so rare to find someone else who likes Italian food.

jokes.text: Artie to Beverly: 'Take over. Don't get drunk.'
jokes.setup: Artie is handing off the desk to deal with the Jeannie situation
jokes.punchline: 'Don't get drunk' as a standard workplace handoff instruction — implying this is a regular enough concern to warrant mentioning
jokes.explanation: Three-word economy joke that does double duty: it's funny as an absurd workplace instruction and it subtly characterizes Beverly. The joke lands on the word 'drunk' which arrives as a complete non-sequitur from 'take over.'

dialogue.speaker: Artie
dialogue.line: No, I'm asking the guy with one eye in row 6. I don't think he knows either.

jokes.text: Larry announces tomorrow's guests, including David Duchovny. Someone off-screen says 'Again? We have David Duchovny again.'
jokes.setup: Larry reads off tomorrow's guest list at the end of the on-air segment
jokes.punchline: An off-screen voice's weary 'Again?' implies Duchovny is a perpetual recycled booking — a winking meta-joke about the show's real casting habits
jokes.explanation: Mild meta-joke that rewards repeat viewers who know Duchovny appears multiple times on the show. The rewatch bonus is real — this is more of an insider wink than a laugh-out-loud moment. Gets a rewatch bonus for the meta-layer.

dialogue.speaker: Artie
dialogue.line: Don't get drunk.

jokes.text: Jeannie looks at a photo on the wall: 'Who is this?' Beverly: 'That's Dana Delany. She was on China Beach.' Jeannie: 'I don't watch TV.'
jokes.setup: Jeannie is waiting backstage, surrounded by photos of TV celebrities
jokes.punchline: 'I don't watch TV' — she's in the greenroom of a TV show her ex-husband hosts and she can't identify a single celebrity on the wall
jokes.explanation: Efficient character establishment for Jeannie — she exists outside Larry's TV-world entirely, which is both funny and poignant. The joke also functions as a subtle dig at Larry: even his own ex-wife finds his world alien and forgettable.

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: Again? We have David duchovny again.

jokes.text: Beverly's reaction/aside about Jeannie: 'He used to get so annoyed that I didn't know who any of the guests were.'
jokes.setup: Jeannie has just confessed she doesn't watch TV, surrounded by celebrity photos
jokes.punchline: She reveals this was an ongoing marital friction point — Larry's TV world constantly bumping up against Jeannie's indifference to it
jokes.explanation: A nice comedic reveal about the marriage — Larry's narcissism extended even to demanding his ex-wife know his guests. It's a small joke but it deepens both characters economically.

dialogue.speaker: Jeannie
dialogue.line: Larry's office hasn't changed a bit.

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: Oh, is, uh, that right?

jokes.text: Hank, after Larry introduces Jeannie to Tatjana: 'Magnificent. The best of Larry. And you, my dear, the best of tatjana.'
jokes.setup: Larry awkwardly introduces his ex-wife to his supermodel dinner date in the backstage hallway
jokes.punchline: Hank sweeps in with a theatrical proclamation treating this social disaster as if it were a highlight reel
jokes.explanation: Very Hank — he turns other people's discomfort into an opportunity to perform. The double 'best of' construction is slightly clunky but still characterful.

dialogue.line: I don't watch TV.

jokes.text: Larry, clearly scrambling to avoid dinner with Jeannie: 'I just have dinner every night with the third guest. It just happens to be tatjana tonight.'
jokes.setup: Larry is trying to explain why he can't have dinner with Jeannie — his ex-wife who's just arrived unannounced
jokes.punchline: The blatantly unconvincing excuse that he 'always' dines with the third guest is transparently false and everyone in the room knows it
jokes.explanation: The joke is Larry's cowardice wrapped in procedural explanation. 'It just happens to be tatjana tonight' is a beautifully lame qualifier. The comedy is in the transparent lie and the fact that everyone — including Jeannie — knows it.

dialogue.speaker: Artie
dialogue.line: The wayans family is in there. A lot of fun going on. Hey, big house party.

jokes.text: Artie: 'You know these supermodels have no stored fat. When they gotta eat, they gotta eat.'
jokes.setup: Jeannie is upset that Larry blew her off to go to dinner with Tatjana
jokes.punchline: Artie explains Larry's choices not with emotional intelligence but with the dietary science of supermodels
jokes.explanation: Classic Artie pragmatism applied to an emotionally charged situation. He's not wrong, which makes it funnier. The biology-as-excuse framing is original and the economy is excellent. Very much a Rip Torn line.

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: Mucho blood, but, you know, not as bad as it looks. Lot of veins in the scalp.

jokes.text: Jeannie, alone with Artie after Larry leaves with Tatjana: 'I can't believe I drove an hour for that.'
jokes.setup: Jeannie made a surprise trip to see Larry, who is now going to dinner with a supermodel
jokes.punchline: Her deflated understatement captures the humiliation perfectly
jokes.explanation: Economical and true. The specificity of 'an hour' makes it funnier than a vague complaint would — she has been calculating the drive time against the emotional return, and the math is brutal.

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: I just have dinner every night with the third guest. It just happens to be tatjana tonight.

jokes.text: Hank, consoling Jeannie: 'You know, I warm 'em up and just... Larry scores.'
jokes.setup: Hank is watching Larry leave with Tatjana while Jeannie is left behind
jokes.punchline: Hank frames the entire dynamic of the show — and apparently his personal life — as him doing the setup work so Larry can get the payoff. The double meaning (warm up the audience / warm up women) is the joke.
jokes.explanation: This is the best joke in the early section of the episode. It's perfectly constructed — Hank's entire professional existential crisis (being the perennial warm-up act) is applied as a sexual metaphor, and it's also an inadvertently accurate description of what he literally does. The character integration is exceptional: only Hank, with his particular brand of oblivious self-pity, would frame sexual rejection this way. Highly quotable, rewatch bonus for the layered meaning.

dialogue.speaker: Tatjana
dialogue.line: Vendela was right. It's so terrific in here.

jokes.text: Jeannie says she's going to get a drink across the street. Hank: 'I'm on the wagon.' Beat — then she ignores this and leaves anyway.
jokes.setup: Jeannie says she needs a drink and invites Hank along
jokes.punchline: Hank announces he's on the wagon — suggesting she shouldn't bother — but the implication is he'll be off it shortly
jokes.explanation: Gets a rewatch bonus because the next scene reveals they went drinking together and slept together — 'I'm on the wagon' is an ironic setup for the entire Hank/Jeannie subplot. On first watch it's a mild beat; in retrospect it's deliciously ironic.

dialogue.speaker: Tatjana
dialogue.line: I can't believe I drove an hour for that.

jokes.text: Jeannie and Hank at a bar. Jeannie: 'He looked right through me.' Hank: 'Oh, I know. It's a cold stare. Yeah, like, um, hi. I'm a star. Who are you?' Jeannie: 'Oh, my God, that's it. You send shivers down my spine.'
jokes.setup: Jeannie and Hank are bonding over being overlooked by Larry
jokes.punchline: Hank's impression of Larry's dismissive star-energy is apparently so accurate it gives Jeannie a physical reaction — both funny and oddly revealing about why she's drawn to these men
jokes.explanation: The comic irony is rich in retrospect — Jeannie is getting 'shivers' from Hank's impression of Larry's narcissism, which is an inadvertently accurate map of her romantic psychology. Funny on first watch; funnier knowing what follows.

dialogue.speaker: Hank
dialogue.line: You know these supermodels have no stored fat. When they gotta eat, they gotta eat.

jokes.text: Hank: 'I also do Cagney, you know.' Then launches into Cagney impression.
jokes.setup: Hank has just done a Larry impression and Jeannie loved it
jokes.punchline: Hank immediately leverages the moment to showcase his full repertoire — the impression-as-seduction-technique, classic oblivious Hank
jokes.explanation: Hank's Cagney detour is endearingly pathetic — he has found an audience and he will not stop performing. The 'you know' tag is a nice character detail, his perpetual insecurity seeking validation.

dialogue.speaker: Hank
dialogue.line: It's so typical. You know, I warm 'em up and just... Larry scores.

jokes.text: Hank's Cagney impression: 'You dirty rat. You killed my brother, see? And now I'm gonna kill you, see?'
jokes.setup: Hank has agreed to do Cagney for Jeannie at the bar
jokes.punchline: The impression itself — the comedy is in Hank doing a full Cagney performance in what is ostensibly a romantic/emotional moment with Larry's ex-wife
jokes.explanation: The impression itself isn't the joke — it's the context. Hank doing Cagney at a bar to seduce his boss's ex-wife is the absurd situation. The craft is moderate because the impression is a generic comedy bit, but character integration saves it.

dialogue.speaker: Jeannie
dialogue.line: He looked right through me.

dialogue.speaker: Hank
dialogue.line: Oh, I know. I know. It's a cold stare.

jokes.text: Cut to the next morning. Jeannie: 'I am... I'm never having another drink again in my life. I got to go.' Hank: 'Oh, Jesus. I have to, uh... I have to go. What?' Then the revelation they clearly slept together.
jokes.setup: The scene cuts from the bar to what is clearly a hotel room the next morning — context slowly dawns
jokes.punchline: The morning-after regret is mutual and wordless, playing out in overlapping half-sentences before either can process what happened
jokes.explanation: The scene break lands the punchline of the previous scene's setup. The comedy is in the horror of both people's dawning realization and their overlapping attempts to flee. It's cringe-comedy done well — the audience processes the implication slightly before the characters do.

dialogue.speaker: Jeannie
dialogue.line: Yeah, like, um, hi. I'm a star. Who are you?

jokes.text: Jeannie: 'Hank, that's my dress.' Hank: 'OK.'
jokes.setup: They are both trying to leave the room in post-coital panic
jokes.punchline: Hank has apparently either picked up or is standing on Jeannie's dress — his 'OK' is the perfect non-response, the comedy of a man who has no idea what to do
jokes.explanation: Two words that carry enormous comedic weight. 'OK' is Hank's entire response to having slept with his boss's ex-wife and now being in possession of her dress. The economy is exceptional — it's a perfect beat of male inadequacy. Highly effective.

dialogue.speaker: Hank
dialogue.line: I also do cagney, you know.

jokes.text: Hank: 'I, uh, I ate everything in the mini bar while you were asleep. I'll send you a check.'
jokes.setup: Hank and Jeannie are in frantic morning-after mode, trying to exit gracefully
jokes.punchline: Hank's revelation that he stress-ate the entire minibar while she slept — and his offer to pay her back — is both pathetically specific and completely in character
jokes.explanation: This is the standout joke of the episode. It's perfectly Hank — the specific detail of eating the entire minibar while Jeannie slept (anxiety eating? hunger? boredom?) combined with his earnest offer to 'send a check' is both deeply pathetic and hilariously specific. Only Hank would do this and only Hank would volunteer the information AND offer financial restitution in the same breath. Strong originality, exceptional character integration, economy is nearly perfect. Comparable to the 8.0 anchor example — sharply observed, specific, highly quotable.

dialogue.speaker: Hank
dialogue.line: His family completely screwed him up. [...] did they spank him?

dialogue.speaker: Jeannie
dialogue.line: Yes. Constantly.

jokes.text: George Washington sketch: Hank trying to deliver the line 'as long as you don't put a beaver in your mouth' and either stumbling or losing the line.
jokes.setup: Artie is directing Hank through a period comedy sketch where he plays a dentist advising George Washington about his wooden teeth
jokes.punchline: The double entendre in 'don't put a beaver in your mouth' combined with Hank being too hungover/distracted to deliver it — he calls for the line
jokes.explanation: The sketch joke (beaver double entendre) is a fairly cheap bit, but the layer of Hank being too compromised to execute it adds some value. The comedy is more in the behind-the-scenes breakdown than the sketch material itself.

dialogue.speaker: Hank
dialogue.line: You dirty rat. You killed my brother, see? And now I'm gonna kill you, see?

jokes.text: Artie coaching Hank through the sketch failure: 'Terrific. You were very good.' Then: 'Hank, buddy, you gotta help me out with this. There's too many lines, or are the words just too big?'
jokes.setup: Hank has just failed to deliver a simple comedy sketch line for the third time
jokes.punchline: Artie's faux-encouraging 'Terrific' followed immediately by 'there's too many lines, or are the words just too big?' — gentle mockery delivered with absolute professional patience
jokes.explanation: Artie at his most Artie — the false encouragement followed by a line that perfectly encapsulates his low opinion of Hank's intelligence. 'Are the words just too big?' is devastating in its breezy delivery. Strong character integration for Artie and for the Artie/Hank dynamic.

dialogue.speaker: Jeannie
dialogue.line: Hank, that's my dress.

jokes.text: Artie asks 'Did she seem happy?' Hank: 'Well, before or after I fucked her?'
jokes.setup: Artie has asked, with genuine concern, whether Jeannie seemed happy — clearly fishing for information
jokes.punchline: Hank's blunt 'Well, before or after I fucked her?' — delivered apparently without guile, as if this is a reasonable clarifying question
jokes.explanation: The best structured joke in the episode. Artie's question is a perfect setup — polite, cautious, trying to maintain plausible deniability — and Hank detonates it with a completely unguarded clarifying question that confirms the worst. The structure is textbook: question → unexpected clarification that reveals the catastrophe. The economy is exceptional (seven words destroy everything). Artie's subsequent silence is the real punchline. This is Hank's obliviousness weaponized — he doesn't understand why this is a problem, which makes it worse. Comparable to the 8.0 anchor; the structure and impact push it higher.

dialogue.speaker: Hank
dialogue.line: I ate everything in the mini bar while you were asleep. I'll send you a check.

jokes.text: Artie's beat of stunned silence after Hank's revelation, followed by: 'I know it wasn't during 'cause you would have been nauseous.'
jokes.setup: Hank has just revealed he slept with Jeannie; Artie is absorbing this
jokes.punchline: Artie's recovery line — rather than expressing horror, he cracks a wry aside about the quality of the experience — is both a tension release and a character moment
jokes.explanation: This is Artie at his absolute finest. Rather than the obvious reaction (shock, anger), he deflects into a deadpan insult about Hank that functions as a displacement mechanism — Artie can't deal with the magnitude of this news so he makes a cutting joke. 'You would have been nauseous' implies so much about Artie's opinion of Hank's attractiveness and the scenario's grotesqueness. Pure Rip Torn delivery.

dialogue.speaker: Hank
dialogue.line: Mr. Washington, you know, these wooden teeth will last a lifetime, as long as you don't put a, uh, Beaver in your mouth.

jokes.text: Phil: 'I can't believe that Hank drilled Jeannie.' Artie: 'Get out of here! No! This way.'
jokes.setup: Phil is being ejected from the rehearsal space after overhearing the Jeannie news
jokes.punchline: Phil can't help editorializing ('drilled Jeannie') on his way out; Artie's 'No! This way!' suggests Phil is trying to exit the wrong way, possibly to tell more people
jokes.explanation: Phil's editorial comment is a functional laugh; Artie misdirecting him is a good physical beat. Not exceptional but it extends the escalation of the previous joke well.

dialogue.speaker: Hank
dialogue.line: There's too many lines, or are the words just too big?

jokes.text: Artie to Hank: 'Sweetheart, baby, trying to ruin us all? Our jobs depend on Larry being just that much better than the other guy.'
jokes.setup: Artie is dealing with the aftermath of Hank's confession, pulling him aside to lecture
jokes.punchline: Artie frames the moral catastrophe of sleeping with Larry's ex-wife entirely in terms of institutional self-interest — not ethics, not loyalty, just: 'this hurts the show'
jokes.explanation: This is the show's core satirical philosophy in one line — everyone's ethics are show business ethics. Artie doesn't care about the betrayal; he cares about the ratings implication. It's funny and dark simultaneously. Strong character integration for Artie.

dialogue.speaker: Hank
dialogue.line: Well, before or after I fucked her?

jokes.text: Artie: 'Ah, forget that! Why did you tell him?' Hank: 'I couldn't help it. He was looking at me.' Artie: 'Oh, God damn you.'
jokes.setup: Artie can't understand why Hank confessed to Larry
jokes.punchline: Hank's explanation — 'He was looking at me' — is a perfect encapsulation of Hank's helplessness under Larry's gaze. He literally cannot maintain a secret when Larry makes eye contact.
jokes.explanation: Hank's 'He was looking at me' is one of the great Hank lines — it perfectly captures his psychology. He has no agency in the face of Larry's attention. The power dynamic of the whole show is in those five words. Artie's 'Oh, God damn you' is the ideal response.

dialogue.speaker: Hank
dialogue.line: I know it wasn't during 'cause you would have been nauseous.

jokes.text: Artie: 'I'll take care of it.' Hank: 'Thanks, Artie.' Artie: 'Oh, shut the fuck up.' Hank: 'Yes, sir.'
jokes.setup: Artie has given Hank his marching orders; Hank is grateful
jokes.punchline: Artie's 'shut the fuck up' in response to a simple 'thanks' — his patience has evaporated — and Hank's obedient 'Yes, sir'
jokes.explanation: The exchange is perfectly calibrated — Artie's irritation boiling over at a thank-you, and Hank's immediate submission ('Yes, sir') is the comic beat. The dynamic of these two is the soul of the show and this is a neat summary of it.

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: What do you mean, she slipped on something and fell onto your penis?

jokes.text: Beverly surprises the writers with a cappuccino machine: Larry 'felt bad that Artie stopped the cappuccino runs so he bought this.' Writer: 'If he feels so bad, why doesn't he pay for the cappuccino runs? He's got the money.'
jokes.setup: Beverly presents the cappuccino machine as a generous gesture from Larry
jokes.punchline: The writer immediately cuts through the PR to the obvious question: a machine is cheaper and more work for them — it's an empty gesture masquerading as generosity
jokes.explanation: The comedy is in the instantly recognizable corporate logic — the boss gives you something that creates more work for you and calls it a gift. Universal and well-observed, though the execution is fairly standard.

dialogue.speaker: Phil
dialogue.line: I can't believe that Hank drilled Jeannie.

jokes.text: Writer: 'That's the problem. I have to make it, then I have to clean it. Or if somebody else makes it, probably I have to clean it.'
jokes.setup: Beverly is extolling the virtues of the cappuccino machine
jokes.punchline: The writer's logical progression — he has to make it AND clean it, and if he doesn't make it, he still has to clean it — is a perfect articulation of the no-win office situation
jokes.explanation: The escalating logic ('or if somebody else makes it, probably I have to clean it') is well-structured. The inevitability of office martyrdom is captured neatly. Solid observational writing.

dialogue.speaker: Artie
dialogue.line: Sweetheart, baby, trying to ruin us all? Our jobs depend on Larry being just that much better than the other guy.

jokes.text: Writer: 'Because it's an empty gesture made in the spirit of cheapness.'
jokes.setup: Beverly is defending the cappuccino machine as a thoughtful gift
jokes.punchline: 'An empty gesture made in the spirit of cheapness' — the perfect phrase for performative corporate generosity
jokes.explanation: This is a genuinely quotable aphorism. 'An empty gesture made in the spirit of cheapness' perfectly describes a specific category of corporate behavior and the phrasing has a rhythm and specificity that elevates it. It could be used in real life. Strong economy and structure.

dialogue.speaker: Beverly
dialogue.line: If he feels so bad, why doesn't he pay for the cappuccino runs? He's got the money.

jokes.text: Larry on-air, reading a fan-sent plate: 'sit down with Hank and Larry.' Hank: 'That is a beautiful plate. But not as beautiful as the plate in your head.'
jokes.setup: They are reading a fan gift — a decorative plate with the show's name on it
jokes.punchline: Hank's 'not as beautiful as the plate in your head' — an abrupt, bizarre insult that doesn't quite track logically but lands as a non-sequitur diss
jokes.explanation: The 'plate in your head' line is an odd joke — it's a bit of a non-sequitur insult that works more because of the audacity than the craft. Moderately funny, slightly confused in execution.

dialogue.speaker: Beverly
dialogue.line: Because it's an empty gesture made in the spirit of cheapness.

jokes.text: Larry on the handmade craft: 'It's nice the inmates get time for arts and crafts.'
jokes.setup: They've received a handmade item from a fan in Corpus Christi, Texas
jokes.punchline: Larry's aside that the craftsmanship suggests the sender is incarcerated
jokes.explanation: A clean talk-show host aside with a slightly dark edge. The economy is excellent and it's a line Larry could plausibly get away with on a real late-night show. The character integration (it feels like something Carson or Letterman might say) is solid.

dialogue.speaker: Hank
dialogue.line: This is a beautiful plate, but not as beautiful as the plate in your head.

jokes.text: The remote control from a fan is demonstrated — it works from much less than 10 feet, apparently zapping someone or something unexpectedly. Larry: 'Oh... that is not... that is not 10 feet!'
jokes.setup: A fan has sent a remote control claiming it works from 10 feet away; they test it on air
jokes.punchline: It fires/activates at close range, apparently hitting someone or causing an unexpected effect — Larry's panicked 'that is not 10 feet!' confirms chaos
jokes.explanation: The transcript indicates something physical happens that we can only infer. The comedy is primarily visual. Gets a rewatch bonus because the visual gag would land much harder on screen. The setup/escalation ('it does work' → 'that is not 10 feet!') is effective.

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: It's nice the inmates get time for arts and crafts.

jokes.text: Post-commercial chaos on set. Larry: 'Wow! Weird vibe, weird vibe. Can you feel it?' Hank: 'All I feel is a slight burning.'
jokes.setup: Larry is trying to re-establish the on-air tone after what was apparently an escalating physical comedy segment
jokes.punchline: Hank's 'slight burning' — which refers to something we can only infer from context but suggests the remote control demo caused physical harm — is a perfect Hank understatement
jokes.explanation: The callback to the remote control gag and the contrast between Larry's metaphysical 'weird vibe' and Hank's literal physical complaint is excellent. The understatement of 'slight burning' is perfectly calibrated Hank.

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: You're a talentless fat fuck, you know that?

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: Wow. I'm sorry? I'm sorry. Did I say... talentless fat fuck, I meant... I meant, uh, sidekick.

jokes.text: Larry apologizes to Hank for Jeannie's visit and says to drop it. Hank: 'I got to tell you though, she was really coming on to me. I really don't want to talk about it.' / 'Even in the marriage, I should've seen the whole thing, because it was obvious that she... she dug me.'
jokes.setup: Larry has just said he doesn't want to talk about Jeannie's visit
jokes.punchline: Hank's inability to drop it, pivoting into a revisionist history where Jeannie had always been attracted to him — the delusional self-aggrandizement is both funny and slightly pitiable
jokes.explanation: Hank rewriting history to make himself the pursued rather than the pursuer is deeply in character. 'She dug me' as a conclusion to his retrospective analysis of the entire marriage is beautifully delusional.

dialogue.speaker: Hank
dialogue.line: So, well, Jeannie tells me you wet your little bed till you were 8?

jokes.text: Larry snaps: 'You know, you're a talentless fat fuck, you know that?' Then immediately: 'I'm sorry? I'm sorry. Did I say... talentless fat fuck, I meant... I meant, uh, sidekick.'
jokes.setup: Hank is pushing Larry's buttons by talking about how Jeannie 'dug him'; Larry's anger breaks through his professional politeness
jokes.punchline: The correction — substituting 'sidekick' for 'talentless fat fuck' — suggests these are synonymous in Larry's mind, which is the real insult
jokes.explanation: The structure here is exceptional. The insult is released in full, then Larry performs a fake apology/correction — and the joke is that 'sidekick' is offered as a synonym, not a replacement. It says everything about how Larry views Hank. The beat of 'Did I say...' buying Larry time to construct the correction adds to the comedy. Strong structure, character integration, and quotability.

dialogue.speaker: Jeannie
dialogue.line: Oh, and fell onto his penis? Just as I suspected.

jokes.text: Hank retaliates: 'Jeannie tells me you wet your little bed till you were 8.'
jokes.setup: Larry has just called Hank a 'talentless fat fuck' (corrected to 'sidekick')
jokes.punchline: Hank deploys the most damaging private information Jeannie shared with him — Larry's childhood bed-wetting — as retaliatory ammunition
jokes.explanation: The reveal that Jeannie and Hank discussed Larry's childhood is both funny and damaging. 'Your little bed' is a perfect detail — the diminutive is cruel. The comedy escalates into something darker and more personal.

dialogue.speaker: Jeannie
dialogue.line: Oh, God! Larry doesn't like white water rafting! Oh, God! Larry doesn't like white water rafting!

jokes.text: Larry and Hank react to the bed-wetting revelation: 'And what else did she say? She said something about... oh, yeah, we're both afraid of white water rafting.'
jokes.setup: Larry is outraged that Jeannie shared his personal secrets with Hank
jokes.punchline: The escalation to 'we're both afraid of white water rafting' is perfect — it's specific, unexpected, and the 'we're both' implies Hank has formed a bond with Larry's ex-wife over shared knowledge of Larry's vulnerabilities
jokes.explanation: The white water rafting detail is the episode's best escalation joke. It's supremely specific — not just a fear, but this particular fear — and the implication that Hank and Jeannie have formed a support group over Larry's phobias is wonderfully absurd. The comedy comes from the specificity and the 'we're both' bonding detail.

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: Thanks for a purr-fect evening? [...] Then it can't be too serious 'cause otherwise, you know, he would've drawn a pony. That's what he's best at.

jokes.text: Larry: 'The... your yogurt's melting.' [after staring Hank down]
jokes.setup: Larry has just silenced Hank with a death stare following the white water rafting revelation
jokes.punchline: The interruption by an assistant noting Larry's yogurt is melting deflates the entire confrontation — Larry's crisis is interrupted by dairy logistics
jokes.explanation: Perfect anti-climax. The yogurt gag punctuates the tension with a mundane intrusion — very Larry Sanders. It's also a nice character beat: Larry is a man whose petty comforts (his yogurt) exist alongside real emotional crises.

dialogue.speaker: Jeannie
dialogue.line: The only reason that I slept with Hank was to hurt you. But... but I don't want you to tell him that, 'cause I don't want to hurt his feelings.

jokes.text: Larry and the woman in his office. She mentions seeing him on the side of a bus. Larry: 'Uh, it was going to el segundo. Oh, yes, yes. How was the picture? Well, it was covered with exhaust but you looked thin.'
jokes.setup: The woman mentions seeing Larry on the side of a bus going to El Segundo
jokes.punchline: 'Covered with exhaust but you looked thin' — the compliment is simultaneously real (he looked thin) and subtly absurd (exhaust as a flattering filter)
jokes.explanation: A small, well-crafted joke about celebrity vanity. Larry's concern is whether the bus ad makes him look thin — not whether the ad is reaching El Segundo demographics. The woman's 'covered with exhaust but you looked thin' threads the needle perfectly.

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: Wow, did you read that off of a greeting card? That was sweet.

jokes.text: Larry to the woman: 'All right, you know what? I'm done. You haven't touched your fish.' / 'I mean I'm done waiting for you to tell me that you slept with Hank.'
jokes.setup: Larry appears to be done with dinner — 'You haven't touched your fish' — suggesting a restaurant setting
jokes.punchline: The misdirect: 'I'm done' appears to be about the dinner; it's actually about waiting for her confession. The fish detail makes the whole confrontation more absurd.
jokes.explanation: Beautifully structured misdirect. 'You haven't touched your fish' sets up a mundane domestic complaint; 'I mean I'm done waiting for you to tell me you slept with Hank' detonates it. The fish detail grounds the absurdity and the delayed patience of 'waiting for you to tell me' implies Larry has been sitting on this information through the whole dinner. Excellent structure and economy.

dialogue.speaker: Hank
dialogue.line: The sun sets at night so it can be at home to watch your monologue.

jokes.text: Jeannie: 'Oh, and fell onto his penis?' — echoing Artie's earlier joke back to Larry.
jokes.setup: Jeannie admits she 'slipped' and Larry uses Artie's earlier 'slipped on something and fell onto his penis' phrasing
jokes.punchline: Jeannie — unprompted — delivers the same punchline ('fell onto his penis'), demonstrating either that this is the obvious response to 'it was an accident' or that she's heard this kind of dismissal from Larry before
jokes.explanation: The callback is slightly implicit — it mirrors Artie's phrasing from the earlier scene. The joke works because both Larry and Jeannie have arrived at the same absurd formulation independently, which itself is a commentary on how predictable these situations are in their world.

dialogue.speaker: Artie
dialogue.line: There they are, the sunshine boys.

jokes.text: Larry: 'Fine, fine. You know what? Who's to say what life is? Maybe you guys are meant to be together. Maybe you're perfect for each other.'
jokes.setup: Larry is furious but trying to perform indifference
jokes.punchline: Larry's theatrical 'who's to say what life is' pseudo-philosophy is transparently not how he feels — the gap between his words and his seething is the joke
jokes.explanation: Classic Larry passive-aggression dressed up as magnanimity. The gap between his performed acceptance and his obvious rage is familiar Larry Sanders territory — well-executed though not exceptional.

dialogue.line: Researchers have found that scuba diving may cause brain damage. Well, there's a shock to the people who watch baywatch.

jokes.text: Larry: 'So I guess when you had an orgasm, you started yelling, "Larry doesn't like white water rafting! Oh, God! Larry doesn't like white water rafting!"'
jokes.setup: Larry is furious that Jeannie shared his personal fears (white water rafting) with Hank during their sexual encounter
jokes.punchline: Larry's hyperbolic imagining of Jeannie yelling his phobia during orgasm is both absurd and devastatingly pointed — it reduces the whole situation to its most undignified essence
jokes.explanation: This is the comedic high point of the episode. It builds perfectly on the white water rafting callback and escalates it to an absurdist extreme. The specificity of 'Larry doesn't like white water rafting' repeated twice mid-climax is perfectly imagined. It reveals Larry's deepest insecurity (that his private fears will be used as currency in others' intimacy) while also being genuinely hilarious. The escalation is earned, the image is unforgettable, and it crystallizes the whole episode's themes — betrayal, vulnerability, Larry's bottomless narcissism — into one deranged sentence. This approaches the 9+ tier.

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: Now there's where you just got to say, 'hey, son, you're grounded.'

jokes.text: Jeannie: 'You know this makes it so clear our marriage didn't work out.'
jokes.setup: Larry has just delivered his white-water-rafting-orgasm speech
jokes.punchline: Jeannie's completely calm, logical conclusion — in the middle of this emotional confrontation — that yes, this confirms the marriage was doomed
jokes.explanation: The perfect button on the scene. Jeannie's deadpan diagnosis — treating Larry's unhinged speech as evidence for a clinical conclusion rather than responding to its emotional content — is both funny and characterful. Economy is nearly perfect.

dialogue.speaker: Jeannie
dialogue.line: Whenever I come to L.A. I get all confused and... and twisted around. L... I hate L.A.

jokes.text: Larry: 'Then it can't be too serious, 'cause otherwise, you know, he would've drawn a pony. That's what he's best at.'
jokes.setup: Jeannie has noted that Hank drew the card
jokes.punchline: Larry's knowledge that Hank's best drawing is a pony — and his use of this as a seriousness barometer — implies Larry has extensive familiarity with Hank's artistic portfolio
jokes.explanation: Exceptional character joke. The idea that Hank has a hierarchy of illustrated animals (ponies for serious occasions, kitty cats for light ones) and that Larry is fluent in this system is both absurd and perfectly specific to this relationship. 'That's what he's best at' as a straight-faced explanation of why a pony would mean more is brilliant. Highly quotable, strong originality.

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: You're marrying someone named stu?

jokes.text: Jeannie: 'The only reason that I slept with Hank was to hurt you. But... but I don't want you to tell him that, 'cause I don't want to hurt his feelings.'
jokes.setup: Jeannie is giving Larry an honest explanation for her night with Hank
jokes.punchline: She openly confesses she used Hank as a weapon against Larry — then immediately pivots to protecting Hank's feelings. The contradiction is the joke.
jokes.explanation: A beautifully structured contradiction. Jeannie instrumentalized Hank for revenge, but she's also kind enough to not want Hank to know he was instrumentalized — which is both sweet and revealing about everyone's delusions. The construction (confession → qualifier) is economical and the irony is rich. Highly quotable.

dialogue.speaker: Artie
dialogue.line: I hope you don't take this the wrong way, but you're never coming back again, are you?

dialogue.speaker: Jeannie
dialogue.line: No.

jokes.text: Larry: 'Hey, I don't want to hurt his feelings either.' [beat] — shared complicity with Jeannie about protecting Hank
jokes.setup: Jeannie has just said she doesn't want Hank to know he was used
jokes.punchline: Larry's immediate agreement — 'I don't want to hurt his feelings either' — the two ex-spouses united in their condescension toward Hank
jokes.explanation: The shared 'poor Hank' moment between Larry and Jeannie is an understated comedic beat — their brief alignment in condescension is the one moment of genuine connection between them, which is its own kind of commentary.

jokes.text: Larry tells Hank: 'Jeannie slept with you because she was trying to hurt me.' Hank: 'Wow. You're really something, aren't you? You just have to get in there and take it away, that special something that happened between she and I.'
jokes.setup: Larry has just told Hank that their night together was a revenge maneuver
jokes.punchline: Hank's response frames Larry as the one being selfish and destructive — for telling the truth — while Hank defends 'that special something' of a drunken revenge hookup as a genuine connection
jokes.explanation: Hank's profound self-delusion is perfectly expressed here. 'That special something that happened between she and I' about a regretted drunken hookup is heartbreaking and funny in equal measure. The character integration is exceptional — only Hank would frame a humiliation as a romance being taken from him.

jokes.text: Larry: 'Oh, that's right, I forgot. I'm sorry. I mean, it's just the universe just revolves around Larry Sanders. The sun sets at night so it can be at home to watch your monologue.'
jokes.setup: Larry has reminded Hank that Jeannie is HIS ex-wife
jokes.punchline: Hank's escalating sarcasm — 'the universe revolves around Larry Sanders' / 'the sun sets at night so it can watch your monologue' — is surprisingly sharp for Hank
jokes.explanation: The cosmological escalation — from universe → sun's daily schedule — is inventive and the image of the sun going home to watch Larry's monologue is a genuinely funny piece of hyperbole. It's also Hank at his most lucid, which adds a layer of comic incongruity.

jokes.text: Artie appears: 'There they are, the sunshine boys.'
jokes.setup: Larry and Hank are in the middle of a bitter argument
jokes.punchline: Artie's cheerful movie-reference entrance — 'The Sunshine Boys' (the Neil Simon play/film about two feuding comedy partners) — lands as both a wry observation and a deadpan reference
jokes.explanation: Artie's 'Sunshine Boys' reference is perfect — it's a literary/cinematic callback to a story about exactly this dynamic (two comedy professionals who hate each other), delivered with maximum economy. The rewatch bonus is for recognizing the Neil Simon reference deepens on reflection. Classic Artie entrance.

jokes.text: Larry: 'I'm not cleaning that.' Artie: 'I'm well aware of that.'
jokes.setup: Artie has just arrived; there is apparently something requiring cleaning — possibly related to the earlier physical comedy
jokes.punchline: Artie's 'I'm well aware of that' — he knows Larry's limits and has already accounted for them
jokes.explanation: A tiny exchange that says everything about Larry and Artie's relationship. Larry's preemptive assertion and Artie's weary confirmation is a miniature portrait of their dynamic — the talent and the handler.

jokes.text: Visual gag/reaction beat: Larry and Hank have clearly been fighting, they're observed by Artie: 'There they are, the sunshine boys.'
jokes.setup: Artie walks in to find Larry and Hank in obvious hostile silence after their argument
jokes.punchline: 'There they are, the sunshine boys' — Artie's dry reference to Neil Simon's comedy about two feuding ex-partners, perfectly applied
jokes.explanation: Artie's 'sunshine boys' is a precise cultural reference (Neil Simon's feuding comedy duo) applied to Larry and Hank with devastating accuracy. It's Artie's voice perfectly — show-business literate, world-weary, cutting. The economy of four words to summarize the dynamic and place it in a comedy tradition is impressive.

jokes.text: Larry burns his mouth on the new cappuccino machine. Beverly: 'Be careful, it's hot!' Larry: 'I told you it was hot.' Beverly: 'Oh, beverly always says it's hot, but it's never that fucking hot.' Beverly: 'Exactly, because we get the good kind from starbucks and they arrive at the perfect temperature.'
jokes.setup: The cappuccino machine has been established as a controversial gift; Larry uses it
jokes.punchline: Larry's self-inflicted burn is the payoff — the machine is indeed worse than the Starbucks runs, which Beverly has been arguing all along. Beverly's vindication is the comedic payoff.
jokes.explanation: The cappuccino machine subplot pays off neatly. Beverly's vindication ('I told you it was hot') and her explanation of why Starbucks is better (temperature consistency) closes the subplot with satisfying logic. Larry burning himself is the physical gag button.

jokes.text: 'Oh, Beverly always says it's hot, but it's never that fucking hot.' / 'Exactly, because we get the good kind from Starbucks and they arrive at the perfect temperature.'
jokes.setup: Larry has burned his mouth and is seeking sympathy
jokes.punchline: Beverly uses his own complaint to prove her original point about Starbucks vs. the machine
jokes.explanation: Beverly's vindication is perfectly timed and structured. Her 'exactly, because we get the good kind from Starbucks' lands as both a factual correction and a 'told you so' — and it makes Larry look cheap AND burned. The resolution of this subplot through the machine hurting him is economically satisfying.

jokes.text: Hank: 'I'm the one who should be gloating. I'm the one who banged his ex-wife.' Artie: 'Actually, neither one of you should be gloating. Big gloater. He's not gloating, he burned his mouth.'
jokes.setup: Beverly says Larry is gloating over being right about the cappuccino machine; Hank escalates by claiming superior gloating rights
jokes.punchline: Artie's patient correction — neither should gloat — followed by the mundane clarification 'he burned his mouth' deflates Hank's drama entirely
jokes.explanation: The convergence of the two subplots (cappuccino machine + Hank/Jeannie) in one absurd scene where Hank is claiming gloating rights over having slept with his boss's ex-wife is very Larry Sanders. Artie's management of both Hank's delusion and Larry's pain is excellent.

jokes.text: On-air segment: 'Researchers have found that scuba diving may cause brain damage. Well, there's a shock to the people who watch Baywatch.'
jokes.setup: Larry is doing a monologue item about a medical research finding on scuba diving
jokes.punchline: The pivot to Baywatch — whose audience Larry implies are already brain-damaged — is a quick, clean late-night joke
jokes.explanation: A standard late-night monologue joke of the era — the Baywatch punchline is competent but not especially original. Gets the job done as a monologue bit, consistent with the show's satirical mimicry of actual late-night material.

jokes.text: On-air segment about a 12-year-old potentially involved in the Oklahoma bombing: 'Now there's where you just got to say, "hey, son, you're grounded."'
jokes.setup: Larry reports on the claim that a 12-year-old may be connected to a terrorist tragedy
jokes.punchline: 'You're grounded' as the appropriate parental response to potential terrorism involvement — reducing the unthinkable to a routine parenting moment
jokes.explanation: A genuinely dark joke that walks the late-night line well. The 'you're grounded' response to potential terrorism involvement is both absurd and on-target as satire of how Americans domesticate tragedy. Economy is excellent. The 1995 context of the Oklahoma bombing reference adds a layer of historical darkness.

jokes.text: Jeannie on the phone with Stu, clearly in Larry's office. She tells him 'nothing' about what she's been doing, while he's been hearing about this all episode. 'Saw some old friends.'
jokes.setup: Jeannie is on the phone with her fiancé Stu, checking in about her trip
jokes.punchline: 'Saw some old friends' as the summary of sleeping with her ex-husband's sidekick — the universe of understatement in that phrase
jokes.explanation: The dramatic irony here is strong — the audience knows exactly what 'saw some old friends' covers for. The economy of the understatement does real work.

jokes.text: Larry asks the woman about 'the question that you asked me.' She responds: 'How's your mouth?' Larry: 'It's not good. I burned myself on the coffee yesterday.' Larry: 'Can't we just get the coffee from starbucks from now on with the little cookie for the chocolate on the tip? I like those.'
jokes.setup: Larry is clearly in a meeting about something important; she redirects to his burned mouth
jokes.punchline: Larry's pivot into an extended monologue about wanting the Starbucks coffee with the chocolate-tipped cookie — his priorities exposed
jokes.explanation: Larry's specific desire for the 'little cookie with the chocolate on the tip' is a great character detail — the man who will fight with his ex-wife over deep emotional wounds but what he really wants is his Starbucks order back. Good character integration.

jokes.text: The long pause between Jeannie saying 'hold on' and her picking the phone back up — inferred visual of her processing what she's going to say
jokes.setup: Jeannie is mid-call with Stu when something interrupts her (presumably Larry or the lobby)
jokes.punchline: A 17-second gap in the transcript — the pause is the joke; she's figuring out how to re-engage with her fiancé after everything that's happened
jokes.explanation: Structural comedy — the joke is entirely in what we imagine is happening during the gap. The silence after a night of chaos with Larry and Hank is funny because of accumulation. Not a traditional joke but characteristic of the show's use of negative space.

jokes.text: Jeannie announces she's engaged. Larry: 'Well, when did you get engaged?' Jeannie: 'At about 11:45 last night.'
jokes.setup: Jeannie has just dropped the bombshell that she's engaged to someone named Stu
jokes.punchline: 'At about 11:45 last night' — the evening she slept with Hank. The timing makes the engagement either a desperate overreaction to or simultaneous with her infidelity
jokes.explanation: One of the best reveals in the episode. 'At about 11:45 last night' lands with the force of a precision strike — the audience calculates immediately that this was after (or around the same time as) her night with Hank. The economy is nearly perfect and the implication is devastating and funny. The specificity of '11:45' makes it feel real.

jokes.text: Larry: 'You're marrying someone named Stu?'
jokes.setup: Jeannie has just announced she's marrying someone named Stu
jokes.punchline: Larry's incredulity focuses entirely on the name — not the engagement, not the timing, just 'Stu' — a beautiful displacement of his real feelings onto the least important detail
jokes.explanation: Four words that do everything. Larry's ego can absorb the loss of Jeannie, but not to someone named Stu. The name becomes a stand-in for Larry's entire jealousy and wounded pride. The economy is exceptional — one incredulous rhetorical question carries enormous emotional weight.

jokes.text: Jeannie: 'And you know, I might even... I might even tell him about all of this some day.' Larry: 'Oh, I wouldn't do that.' Jeannie: 'Well, you're right. You wouldn't.'
jokes.setup: Jeannie is saying she might eventually tell Stu about her L.A. adventure
jokes.punchline: Larry's 'I wouldn't do that' (offered as wisdom/advice) is immediately turned back on him — 'Well, you're right. You wouldn't' — exposing his advice as self-interested rather than wise
jokes.explanation: This is a perfectly structured exchange. Larry's advice ('I wouldn't do that') sounds wise; Jeannie's comeback ('Well, you're right. You wouldn't') instantly recontextualizes it — Larry's advice is autobiography, not wisdom. He's incapable of honesty with partners. The exchange is tight, earned, and character-rich.

jokes.text: Larry, after Jeannie leaves: 'Wow, wow, wow, wow, wow, wow, wow.' [extended beat]
jokes.setup: Jeannie has just left, dropping the engagement bomb
jokes.punchline: Larry's inarticulate 'wow' repeated seven times — he has no words for what just happened
jokes.explanation: The repeated 'wow' is characterful and understated — Larry reduced to a single word looped. It's a beat that requires the performance to work fully but reads as a good moment in the transcript.

jokes.text: Hank, after Jeannie leaves: 'You were married to that whacko for 3 years? Can you believe that?'
jokes.setup: Jeannie has just exited after the engagement revelation
jokes.punchline: Hank calling Jeannie a 'whacko' — the man who slept with her the previous night and called it 'that special something' is now characterizing her as unstable
jokes.explanation: The callback to Hank's earlier romanticization of his night with Jeannie makes this a perfect ironic reversal. He went from defending 'that special something' to 'that whacko' in about ten minutes of screen time. Classic Hank — his feelings are entirely situational.

jokes.text: Artie says goodbye to Jeannie backstage: 'I hope it did some good.' Artie: 'I think, my dear, it was something only you could lay to rest, so to speak.'
jokes.setup: Artie is saying goodbye to Jeannie, reflecting on her visit
jokes.punchline: 'Only you could lay to rest, so to speak' — 'lay' doing double duty as both 'put to rest' and the sexual act she performed with Hank
jokes.explanation: Artie's pun is perfectly delivered — the 'so to speak' tags the double meaning with just enough wink without explaining it. Only Artie would send someone off with a pun about their sexual encounter. Elegant and very much in character for Rip Torn's Artie.

jokes.text: Artie presents Jeannie with the cappuccino machine as a farewell gift. 'Stu loves cappuccino.' Artie: 'I'm sure he does, and Jeannie, sweetheart, I hope you don't take this the wrong way, but you're never coming back again, are you?' Jeannie: 'No.'
jokes.setup: Artie is giving Jeannie the cappuccino machine as a parting gift from the show
jokes.punchline: Artie's direct, almost tender confirmation that she should never return — phrased as a gentle wish — is both the institutional and emotional close of the episode
jokes.explanation: A masterful closing beat. The cappuccino machine — the episode's B-plot object — becomes the farewell gift that closes both plotlines simultaneously. Artie's gentle 'you're never coming back again, are you?' is the most Artie possible combination of institutional pragmatism and genuine warmth. Jeannie's quiet 'No' is the perfect button. High character integration, excellent structure, and it lands as the emotional and comedic close of the episode.

jokes.text: Artie presents the cappuccino machine as a going-away gift to Jeannie. 'Stu loves cappuccino.' / 'I'm sure he does.'
jokes.setup: Artie gives Jeannie a farewell gift — the cappuccino machine
jokes.punchline: 'Stu loves cappuccino' — she immediately has a use for the thing that caused so much drama; 'I'm sure he does' from Artie is perfectly dry
jokes.explanation: A wonderful resolution to the cappuccino B-plot. Artie getting rid of the source of conflict (the machine) by giving it to Jeannie is both a practical solution and a comedic one. 'Stu loves cappuccino' reveals that the machine is going to a good home (Stu, the man whose fiancée just slept with someone else), which layers the joke beautifully. 'I'm sure he does' from Artie — knowing everything — is the perfect dry close.

jokes.text: Artie to Jeannie: 'I hope you don't take this the wrong way, but you're never coming back again, are you?' Jeannie: 'No.'
jokes.setup: Artie is saying goodbye to Jeannie
jokes.punchline: He asks her — with total sincerity — if she's never coming back, framed as if it might be taken the wrong way but clearly being asked with hope
jokes.explanation: The episode's most elegant closing joke. 'I hope you don't take this the wrong way, but you're never coming back again, are you?' is the perfect Artie line: it's ostensibly diplomatic ('I hope you don't take this the wrong way') while being completely blunt about wanting her gone. The 'No' from Jeannie — delivered without hurt, just agreement — completes the joke beautifully. It's warm and ruthless simultaneously, which is exactly the show's register. The economy is nearly flawless.

tmdb_overview: A surprise visit by Larry's ex-wife causes an unusual triangle between her, Larry and Hank. Larry offers a cappuccino machine as a substitute for the daily office run to Starbucks.
